specPoints.text: practical: investigate the energy content in a food sample

primer.text: You know food stores energy and that burning releases it. This practical measures that release directly: burn a weighed food sample under a known mass of water, read the temperature rise, and convert it into joules per gram — then judge how much of the heat the simple setup actually lost.

lessons.title: Burning Food to Measure Energy
sourceHeadings: Practical: Energy Content of a Food Sample
Investigating the energy content of food samples diagram
lessons.opening: A simple calorimetry experiment compares the energy stored in foods. Twenty-five cubic centimetres of water sit in a boiling tube, a weighed food sample burns beneath it, and the temperature rise tells you the energy transferred. Dividing by the sample's mass turns the reading into joules per gram, comparable across popcorn, walnuts or crisps.
keyPoints: Twenty-five cubic centimetres of water are measured into the boiling tube.
The starting temperature of the water is recorded before burning.
The food sample is weighed, burned completely, and held two centimetres from the tube.
The final water temperature is recorded after the sample stops burning.
Energy per gram equals mass of water times temperature rise times four point two, divided by sample mass.
Incomplete burning and heat loss both make the calculated values underestimates.

low.restatement: Burn food under water; bigger temperature rise, more energy.
low.analogy: Boiling a kettle on a campfire: the fire's heat shows up on the thermometer.
low.examPointer: Quote the equation with all four variables when calculating.

medium.restatement: The method is a crude calorimeter: every joule the water misses went to the air or stayed unburnt.
medium.analogy: Measuring a shower's heat from the bathwater alone.
medium.examPointer: Explain both limitations and their fixes — relight and shield with foil.

check.stem: What is measured to compare the energy content of two foods?

options.text: The temperature rise of a fixed mass of water heated by each burning sample
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: The mass lost by the burning food
options.explanation: Mass loss alone is not the read-out.

options.text: The time the food takes to burn
options.explanation: Duration is not the measure of energy.

options.text: The flame's colour
options.explanation: Colour indicates completeness, not energy.

check.stem: Why must the sample burn completely?

options.text: Unburnt food holds energy that never reached the water, skewing the value low
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Because smoke is toxic to the water
options.explanation: Toxicity is not the measurement concern.

options.text: Because the balance requires ash
options.explanation: The sample mass is taken before burning.

options.text: Because the thermometer stops working in smoke
options.explanation: Smoke does not disable the thermometer.

check.stem: Which value is four point two in the equation?

options.text: The specific heat capacity of water
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: The density of water
options.explanation: Density is one gram per cubic centimetre.

options.text: The energy content of the food
options.explanation: That is the unknown being calculated.

options.text: The mass of the sample
options.explanation: The sample mass is measured separately.

check.stem: In the results table, which sample released more energy per gram?

options.text: The walnut, at about 177.6 joules per gram versus popcorn's 132.2
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: The popcorn, whose mass was larger
options.explanation: Popcorn's 8.5 grams is actually heavier than the walnut's 8.1.

options.text: Both released the same energy
options.explanation: Their temperature rises differ clearly.

options.text: Neither released measurable energy
options.explanation: Both rows show sizable temperature rises.

check.stem: Why does the calculated value underestimate the true energy content?

options.text: Some heat escapes to the surroundings and some food may not burn fully
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Because water absorbs energy too fast
options.explanation: Absorption is exactly what is measured.

options.text: Because thermometers read too high
options.explanation: Underestimation comes from losses, not misreadings.

options.text: Because food has no real energy content
options.explanation: The results table shows real values.

check.stem: State the equation for energy transferred per gram of food.
check.modelAnswer: Mass of water times temperature increase times four point two, divided by the mass of the food sample.

check.stem: Name one improvement that reduces heat loss in this experiment.
check.modelAnswer: Moving the boiling tube nearer to the burning food, or shielding the tube with aluminium foil.

check.stem: Explain why a larger temperature rise indicates a more energy-dense food.
check.modelAnswer: Because the water's temperature rise is proportional to the energy the burning sample released; with the same water mass and setup, a sample that warms the water more must have transferred more joules per gram burnt.

check.stem: A sample of 8.5 g popcorn warms 25 g of water by 10.7 °C. Show the energy per gram is about 132 J.
check.modelAnswer: Twenty-five times ten point seven times four point two gives about 1123.5 joules; divided by eight point five grams, the energy transferred per gram of food is roughly 132.2 joules per gram, matching the results table.

glossary.definition: Measuring energy by the temperature change it produces in a known mass of water.
The energy needed to raise one kilogram of water by one degree Celsius; 4.2 kJ for water.
Combustion that fails to release all the sample's stored energy, skewing results low.
